passages.title: The Back Page
passages.text:
The week the music shop closed, my uncle Arno asked me to help him count everything. Not to sell it, he said. The new owners of the building would take the display cases, and a dealer from the city would take the stock. He only wanted to know what had been there.

So for five days I stood on the rolling ladder and read numbers down to him: forty-two packs of violin strings, eleven boxes of clarinet reeds, one accordion left from a polka craze nobody remembered. He wrote each number in the old green ledger he had kept behind the counter for decades, in handwriting so small and even it looked printed. When I asked why it mattered, since nobody was going to read the ledger, he said, "I'll read it," and went on writing.

On the fourth afternoon a man came in carrying a dented trumpet wrapped in a bath towel. He was only a few years younger than Arno, and he set the trumpet on the counter as if it might break. He had borrowed it, he said, in 1987, to play in his high school's spring concert, and had meant to bring it back the following Monday. He had heard the store was closing. He thought he had better hurry.

Arno unwrapped the trumpet and turned it over. I expected him to laugh, or to tell the man to keep it; it was a cheap student model, and its valves were stuck. Instead he opened the ledger to the back page, found a line I had not seen him write, and drew a neat stroke through it. Then he thanked the man, and the man left, and Arno went back to the numbers as if nothing had happened.

I climbed down from the ladder and looked at the back page. It was a list, in the same tiny hand, of things that had gone out the door and not come back: a cello, two flutes, a music stand, a trumpet. Each line had a name beside it and a date. Some were thirty years old. Only the trumpet had been crossed out.

"You kept track of all of these?" I asked.

"Somebody had to," he said. He did not look up. "People always mean to bring things back."

On the last day we locked the door at noon. Arno put the ledger under his arm, and he did not offer to let me carry it.
